sentences.text: Pamparaptor is an extinct paravian theropod dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous of Argentine Patagonia. It is a basal dromaeosaurid with feet similar to those of troodontids. The animal had a metatarsal measuring approximately 9.3 cm in length.

The only known species, P. micros, is represented by a single fossilized left foot featuring a distinctive killing claw. Later researchers estimated the animal's length at about 1.15 meters and its weight at 2.6 kilograms. The species name micros means "small" and refers to the specimen's estimated length of 0.5 to 0.7 meters.
The specimen was initially thought to be a juvenile or subadult of the related genus Neuquenraptor because it was much smaller and shared similarities with it.
Its most striking feature is a single fossilized left foot featuring a distinctive killing claw.

The sole specimen was discovered in 2005 by technician Diego Rosales while working for the Lake Barreales Paleontological Center. The fossil was found at the Baal Quarry, an outcrop of the Portezuelo Formation dated to the late Turonian or early Coniacian. Fossils of Pamparaptor were found in Neuquén Province, Patagonia, Argentina. The specimen was recovered from the Portezuelo Formation, part of the Río Neuquén Subgroup of the Neuquén Group. The species is known from holotype MUCPv-1163, an articulated and nearly complete left foot.

The genus was formally described in 2010 by a team including Juan Porfiri, Jorge Calvo, and Domenica Dos Santos. The genus Pamparaptor was named by Juan D. Porfiri, Jorge O. Calvo, and Domenica dos Santos in 2011. The genus authority for Pamparaptor is Porfiri, Calvo & Santos, 2011.
The fossil-bearing environment was an alluvial fan composed of mudstones, siltstones, and claystones.

While its precise classification remains uncertain, the original authors argued that it belongs to the dromaeosaurid family. Pamparaptor belongs to the family Dromaeosauridae. The parent group of Pamparaptor is Deinonychosauria.

The authors rejected the hypothesis that the related genus Neuquenraptor was a junior synonym of Unenlagia. A 2024 study recovered Pamparaptor as an unenlagiine, but also as a sister taxon to anchiornithids, troodontids, and microraptorian dromaeosaurids.

The Portezuelo Formation, where the fossil was found, was deposited from the late Turonian to the early Coniacian. Pamparaptor lived during the late Cretaceous, specifically the Turonian and Coniacian stages, approximately 89 million years ago. The time range for Pamparaptor is from the Turonian to the Coniacian, between 93.9 and 85.7 million years ago.
Researchers have debated whether Pamparaptor might have affinities with troodontids due to similarities in foot anatomy.
